title: Active Portfolio Management: A Quantitative Approach for Producing Superior Returns and Selecting Superior Returns and Controlling Risk
author: Richard C. Grinold, Ronald N. Kahn
notes: Central framework: alpha/residual return is evaluated against active risk through information ratio and value added. Ch. 5 residual risk/return and Ch. 6 Fundamental Law.

title: Active Portfolio Management: A Quantitative Approach for Producing Superior Returns and Selecting Superior Returns and Controlling Risk
author: Richard C. Grinold, Ronald N. Kahn
notes: Repeatedly frames active management as maximizing expected active return while penalizing active/residual risk. Ch. 4, Ch. 5, Ch. 12.

title: Active Portfolio Management: A Quantitative Approach for Producing Superior Returns and Selecting Superior Returns and Controlling Risk
author: Richard C. Grinold, Ronald N. Kahn
notes: Strong active-vs-benchmark framing: hold benchmark when forecasts match consensus; active management exists when forecasts differ. Ch. 2 and Ch. 16.

title: Active Portfolio Management: A Quantitative Approach for Producing Superior Returns and Selecting Superior Returns and Controlling Risk
author: Richard C. Grinold, Ronald N. Kahn
notes: Portfolio construction converts alphas, covariance estimates, costs, and risk aversion into active holdings. Ch. 12.

title: Active Portfolio Management: A Quantitative Approach for Producing Superior Returns and Selecting Superior Returns and Controlling Risk
author: Richard C. Grinold, Ronald N. Kahn
notes: Teaches factor exposures, benchmark/cash neutrality, control variables, sector and size exposure matching, and avoiding unintended concentration. Ch. 3, 11, 12, 14.

title: Active Portfolio Management: A Quantitative Approach for Producing Superior Returns and Selecting Superior Returns and Controlling Risk
author: Richard C. Grinold, Ronald N. Kahn
notes: Formalizes the active management process from raw information to refined forecasts to portfolio construction; Fundamental Law defines skill/breadth constraints. Ch. 1, 6, 10, 16.

title: Active Portfolio Management: A Quantitative Approach for Producing Superior Returns and Selecting Superior Returns and Controlling Risk
author: Richard C. Grinold, Ronald N. Kahn
notes: Covers information analysis, performance evaluation with t-statistics/IR/IC, data-mining controls, and out-of-sample testing. Ch. 11.

title: Active Portfolio Management: A Quantitative Approach for Producing Superior Returns and Selecting Superior Returns and Controlling Risk
author: Richard C. Grinold, Ronald N. Kahn
notes: execution_quality_and_trade_implementation

title: Active Portfolio Management: A Quantitative Approach for Producing Superior Returns and Selecting Superior Returns and Controlling Risk
author: Richard C. Grinold, Ronald N. Kahn
notes: Covers performance analysis: distinguishing skill from luck, attribution, identifying which bets worked, and improving the investment process. Ch. 14

title: Active Portfolio Management: A Quantitative Approach for Producing Superior Returns and Selecting Superior Returns and Controlling Risk
author: Richard C. Grinold, Ronald N. Kahn
notes: Present through turnover, moving from current to target portfolio, and value-added/turnover tradeoffs, but not classic periodic rebalancing. Ch. 13.

title: Active Portfolio Management: A Quantitative Approach for Producing Superior Returns and Selecting Superior Returns and Controlling Risk
author: Richard C. Grinold, Ronald N. Kahn
notes: Secondary coverage through market microstructure, liquidity suppliers, inventory risk, trade size, urgency, spreads, market impact, and costs. Ch. 13.

title: Active Portfolio Management: A Quantitative Approach for Producing Superior Returns and Selecting Superior Returns and Controlling Risk
author: Richard C. Grinold, Ronald N. Kahn
notes: Present through breadth, independent forecasts, diversified active bets, and factor-model diversification, but not mainly retail asset-allocation diversification. Ch. 6-7.

title: Active Portfolio Management: A Quantitative Approach for Producing Superior Returns and Selecting Superior Returns and Controlling Risk
author: Richard C. Grinold, Ronald N. Kahn
notes: CAPM, consensus expected returns, benchmark efficiency logic, and EMH are discussed, but price formation itself is not deeply taught. Ch. 2 and 14.

title: Active Portfolio Management: A Quantitative Approach for Producing Superior Returns and Selecting Superior Returns and Controlling Risk
author: Richard C. Grinold, Ronald N. Kahn
notes: Valuation appears through DDM, risk-adjusted expectations, growth forecasts, and implied growth rates, but is secondary to active portfolio management. Ch. 8-9.

title: Technical Analysis of Stock Trends
author: Robert D. Edwards, John Magee, W.H.C. Bassetti
notes: Central coverage. Ch. 6-12 teach reversal patterns, H&S, triangles, rectangles, double/triple tops, broadening formations, diamonds, wedges, flags, pennants, and gaps; Ch. 33 tactical review.

title: Technical Analysis of Stock Trends
author: Robert D. Edwards, John Magee, W.H.C. Bassetti
notes: Central coverage. Ch. 14-15 teach trendlines, channels, uptrends/downtrends, penetration validity, throwbacks, corrective trends, and major trend channels; Ch. 29 applies trendlines.

title: Technical Analysis of Stock Trends
author: Robert D. Edwards, John Magee, W.H.C. Bassetti
notes: Ch. 13 is directly on support/resistance: definitions, role reversal, volume, locating levels, break implications, round numbers, historical levels, and panic moves; Ch. 30 applies levels to entries/stops.

title: Technical Analysis of Stock Trends
author: Robert D. Edwards, John Magee, W.H.C. Bassetti
notes: Volume is repeatedly taught for pattern confirmation and interpretation: H&S in Ch. 6, triangles in Ch. 8, support/resistance in Ch. 13, and volume signals in Ch. 28.

title: Technical Analysis of Stock Trends
author: Robert D. Edwards, John Magee, W.H.C. Bassetti
notes: Teaches regime identification through Dow Theory and bull/bear trend phases in Ch. 3-5.1, plus Magee Evaluative Index for bull/bear tops and bottoms in Ch. 38.

title: Technical Analysis of Stock Trends
author: Robert D. Edwards, John Magee, W.H.C. Bassetti
notes: Ch. 27 is devoted to stop orders, including protective stops, stop levels, stop distances, and progressive stops; Ch. 30 covers placing stops; Ch. 34 summarizes when to get out.

title: Technical Analysis of Stock Trends
author: Robert D. Edwards, John Magee, W.H.C. Bassetti
notes: Direct trade sizing coverage: Ch. 26 determining trade size and risk; Ch. 40 capital to use in trading; Ch. 42 formula using entry, stop, risk factor, capital, and risk per trade.

title: Technical Analysis of Stock Trends
author: Robert D. Edwards, John Magee, W.H.C. Bassetti
notes: Ch. 20 covers leverage, Ch. 25 margin and short selling, Ch. 41 composite leverage by market condition, and Appendix B discusses composite leverage and greater risk from margin.

title: Technical Analysis of Stock Trends
author: Robert D. Edwards, John Magee, W.H.C. Bassetti
notes: Ch. 42 covers portfolio risk posture, over/undertrading, risk per trade, single-stock risk, portfolio risk and measurement, plus reducing overexposure by hedging or eliminating positions.

title: Technical Analysis of Stock Trends
author: Robert D. Edwards, John Magee, W.H.C. Bassetti
notes: Ch. 22 covers diversification in stock selection, Ch. 31 "Not All in One Basket" covers diversification costs/benefits, and Ch. 38 covers balanced and diversified posture.

title: Technical Analysis of Stock Trends
author: Robert D. Edwards, John Magee, W.H.C. Bassetti
notes: Teaches rule-based technical trading through Ch. 28 Three Days Away Rule and basing points, Ch. 30 support/resistance buying rules, Ch. 33 tactical review, and Ch. 34 tactical summary.

title: Technical Analysis of Stock Trends
author: Robert D. Edwards, John Magee, W.H.C. Bassetti
notes: Part 2 is Trading Tactics. Ch. 18-24 cover tactical problem, chart/data preparation, stock selection, high-risk stock management, probable moves; Ch. 29 applies to buy/sell/short/cover.

title: Technical Analysis of Stock Trends
author: Robert D. Edwards, John Magee, W.H.C. Bassetti
notes: Present but secondary. Ch. 36 covers moving averages and appendix/glossary mentions MACD, RSI, OBV, Bollinger Bands, stochastics; main emphasis is classical chart analysis.

title: Technical Analysis of Stock Trends
author: Robert D. Edwards, John Magee, W.H.C. Bassetti
notes: Present inside Ch. 42 risk-management framework: average drawdown, maximum drawdown, realized losses, profit/loss ratios, and portfolio risk stats, but not a standalone major topic.

title: International Financial Statement Analysis
author: Thomas R. Robinson, Elaine Henry, Wendy L. Pirie, Michael A. Broihahn
notes: Core concept. Structured around FSA: Ch. 1 framework, Ch. 4 income statement, Ch. 5 balance sheet, Ch. 6 cash flow, Ch. 7 analysis techniques, Ch. 9 applications, Ch. 17 reporting quality.

title: International Financial Statement Analysis
author: Thomas R. Robinson, Elaine Henry, Wendy L. Pirie, Michael A. Broihahn
notes: Strong chapter-level coverage of revenue/expense recognition, EPS, income statement ratios, profitability ratios, DuPont analysis, and forecasting future net income/cash flow. Ch. 4, 7, 9.

title: International Financial Statement Analysis
author: Thomas R. Robinson, Elaine Henry, Wendy L. Pirie, Michael A. Broihahn
notes: Present as an FSA application rather than full valuation text. Covers valuation ratios, market-based valuation inputs, and screening for equity investments. Ch. 7 and Ch. 9.

title: International Financial Statement Analysis
author: Thomas R. Robinson, Elaine Henry, Wendy L. Pirie, Michael A. Broihahn
notes: Secondary coverage. Discusses projections of future performance, FCFF/FCFE, and valuation implications, but full intrinsic valuation methodology is not central. Ch. 6 and Ch. 9.

title: International Financial Statement Analysis
author: Thomas R. Robinson, Elaine Henry, Wendy L. Pirie, Michael A. Broihahn
notes: Teaches evaluation of company performance, profitability, cash generation, segment performance, and accounting/management quality; moat/competitive advantage is not central. Ch. 7, 9, 17.

title: International Financial Statement Analysis
author: Thomas R. Robinson, Elaine Henry, Wendy L. Pirie, Michael A. Broihahn
notes: Covers financial assets/liabilities, equity, bonds, leases, debt with equity features, intercorporate investments, and securities, but from accounting/analysis angle. Ch. 5, 13, 15.

title: International Financial Statement Analysis
author: Thomas R. Robinson, Elaine Henry, Wendy L. Pirie, Michael A. Broihahn
notes: Covers firm-level credit/debt analysis: solvency ratios, credit analysis, rating process, long-term debt, covenants, leases, and off-balance-sheet financing; not crisis-focused. Ch. 7, 9, 13.

title: International Financial Statement Analysis
author: Thomas R. Robinson, Elaine Henry, Wendy L. Pirie, Michael A. Broihahn
notes: Covers foreign currency transactions, FX exposure, translation of foreign-currency statements, and hyperinflationary economies; not broad global macro investing. Ch. 16.

title: Stocks for the Long Run: The Definitive Guide to Financial Market Returns & Long-Term Investment Strategies, Sixth Edition
author: Jeremy J. Siegel
notes: Central comparison of stocks, bonds, bills, gold, commodities, and real returns in Ch. 1; Ch. 15 also explains stock index futures, index options, and SPDRs.

title: Stocks for the Long Run: The Definitive Guide to Financial Market Returns & Long-Term Investment Strategies, Sixth Edition
author: Jeremy J. Siegel
notes: Ch. 2 directly teaches risk/return measurement, holding-period risk, stock-bond correlation, efficient frontiers, and risk-return tradeoffs across portfolio mixes.

title: Stocks for the Long Run: The Definitive Guide to Financial Market Returns & Long-Term Investment Strategies, Sixth Edition
author: Jeremy J. Siegel
notes: Ch. 2 gives recommended stock allocations by risk tolerance and holding period; Ch. 20 applies long-run portfolio structuring.

title: Stocks for the Long Run: The Definitive Guide to Financial Market Returns & Long-Term Investment Strategies, Sixth Edition
author: Jeremy J. Siegel
notes: Core thesis is long-horizon equity investing; Ch. 2 treats holding periods and Ch. 20 is explicitly about structuring portfolios for long-term growth.

title: Stocks for the Long Run: The Definitive Guide to Financial Market Returns & Long-Term Investment Strategies, Sixth Edition
author: Jeremy J. Siegel
notes: Ch. 2 covers stock-bond diversification through correlation and efficient frontiers; Ch. 9 covers global diversification, foreign equities, correlations, and optimal foreign allocation.

title: Stocks for the Long Run: The Definitive Guide to Financial Market Returns & Long-Term Investment Strategies, Sixth Edition
author: Jeremy J. Siegel
notes: Ch. 1 uses real returns and purchasing power; Ch. 11 centrally covers stocks as inflation hedges, short-term inflation weakness, rates, and inflation distortions.

title: Stocks for the Long Run: The Definitive Guide to Financial Market Returns & Long-Term Investment Strategies, Sixth Edition
author: Jeremy J. Siegel
notes: Ch. 10 covers money, gold, central banks, Federal Reserve money creation, and how the Fed affects interest rates; Ch. 14 links economic data to Fed policy.

title: Stocks for the Long Run: The Definitive Guide to Financial Market Returns & Long-Term Investment Strategies, Sixth Edition
author: Jeremy J. Siegel
notes: Ch. 12 is directly titled Stocks and the Business Cycle and covers business-cycle dating, stock returns around turning points, cycle timing, and prediction difficulty.

title: Stocks for the Long Run: The Definitive Guide to Financial Market Returns & Long-Term Investment Strategies, Sixth Edition
author: Jeremy J. Siegel
notes: Ch. 14 covers stocks, bonds, and economic data: market reaction principles, employment reports, inflation reports, core inflation, employment costs, and Fed policy.

title: Stocks for the Long Run: The Definitive Guide to Financial Market Returns & Long-Term Investment Strategies, Sixth Edition
author: Jeremy J. Siegel
notes: Ch. 5 covers P/E, book value, Tobin's Q, market value to GDP, and valuation sentiment; Ch. 6 covers P/E and P/B value criteria; Ch. 7 discusses justified P/E for growth stocks.

title: Stocks for the Long Run: The Definitive Guide to Financial Market Returns & Long-Term Investment Strategies, Sixth Edition
author: Jeremy J. Siegel
notes: Ch. 19 directly evaluates funds, managers, beating the market, underperformance, costs, and the practical case for low-cost market-matching strategies.

title: Stocks for the Long Run: The Definitive Guide to Financial Market Returns & Long-Term Investment Strategies, Sixth Edition
author: Jeremy J. Siegel
notes: Present through Ch. 5 on dividends, earnings, shareholder value, economic growth, earnings growth and P/E, plus Ch. 7 on earnings-growth valuation; not a company-level profitability manual.

title: Stocks for the Long Run: The Definitive Guide to Financial Market Returns & Long-Term Investment Strategies, Sixth Edition
author: Jeremy J. Siegel
notes: Ch. 9 covers global investing, foreign stock returns, exchange-rate risk, dollar risk, FX hedging, and the European exchange-rate mechanism, but secondary to long-run equity thesis.

title: Stocks for the Long Run: The Definitive Guide to Financial Market Returns & Long-Term Investment Strategies, Sixth Edition
author: Jeremy J. Siegel
notes: Ch. 15 explains futures margin, leverage, SPDRs, options, hedging, and risks of controlling large stock exposure with little capital; useful but not central.

title: Stocks for the Long Run: The Definitive Guide to Financial Market Returns & Long-Term Investment Strategies, Sixth Edition
author: Jeremy J. Siegel
notes: Ch. 17 tests moving-average strategies and backtests the 200-day moving average; Ch. 18 examines calendar anomalies, but this is empirical evaluation rather than full system design.

title: Technical Analysis
author: Charles D. Kirkpatrick II, Julie R. Dahlquist
notes: Ch. 2 is The Basic Principle of Technical Analysis-The Trend; Part III is Trend Analysis; Ch. 12 teaches trend basics, directional trends, channels, retracements, and trend lines.

title: Technical Analysis
author: Charles D. Kirkpatrick II, Julie R. Dahlquist
notes: Ch. 12 directly teaches trading ranges, support/resistance, reversal points, channels, pullbacks/throwbacks, speed lines, and support/resistance projections; Ch. 13 extends into breakouts and stops.

title: Technical Analysis
author: Charles D. Kirkpatrick II, Julie R. Dahlquist
notes: Part IV is dedicated to chart pattern analysis: bar chart patterns, point-and-figure patterns, short-term patterns, gaps, reversals, volatility patterns, intraday patterns, and candlesticks.

title: Technical Analysis
author: Charles D. Kirkpatrick II, Julie R. Dahlquist
notes: Ch. 6 includes Importance of Volume; Ch. 18 covers trend confirmation through volume, volume statistics, volume oscillators, volume spikes, and open interest.

title: Technical Analysis
author: Charles D. Kirkpatrick II, Julie R. Dahlquist
notes: Ch. 8 covers breadth/strength indicators; Ch. 14 covers moving averages, directional movement, envelopes, channels, and bands; Ch. 18 covers momentum, confirmation, and oscillators.

title: Technical Analysis
author: Charles D. Kirkpatrick II, Julie R. Dahlquist
notes: Teaches market-state classification through Dow Theory, primary/secondary/minor trends, trading ranges, breadth, market strength, cycles, and market/issue selection.

title: Technical Analysis
author: Charles D. Kirkpatrick II, Julie R. Dahlquist
notes: Ch. 9 covers temporal patterns/cycles including Kondratieff waves, historical, presidential, election, and seasonal patterns; Ch. 19 is a full chapter on cycle analysis/projections.

title: Technical Analysis
author: Charles D. Kirkpatrick II, Julie R. Dahlquist
notes: Ch. 22 System Design and Testing covers why systems are necessary, discretionary vs nondiscretionary systems, system design requirements, initial decisions, and types of technical systems.

title: Technical Analysis
author: Charles D. Kirkpatrick II, Julie R. Dahlquist
notes: Ch. 22 covers system testing, data, optimization, and robustness; Ch. 23 extends to portfolio-system testing and Monte Carlo simulation for risk of ruin/drawdown resilience.

title: Technical Analysis
author: Charles D. Kirkpatrick II, Julie R. Dahlquist
notes: Ch. 13 covers entry/exit stops, protective stops, trailing stops, time stops, money stops, stops after gaps, and false-breakout stops; Ch. 23 also includes exit strategies.

title: Technical Analysis
author: Charles D. Kirkpatrick II, Julie R. Dahlquist
notes: Ch. 23 directly frames money management around trade size, contracts/shares/dollars, and says money management is also called position sizing, tied to stops, diversification, and execution.

title: Technical Analysis
author: Charles D. Kirkpatrick II, Julie R. Dahlquist
notes: Ch. 13 includes calculating a risk/return ratio for breakout trading; Ch. 23 covers reward-to-risk, risk definition, money-management risks, and risk-control methods.

title: Technical Analysis
author: Charles D. Kirkpatrick II, Julie R. Dahlquist
notes: Present but secondary. Ch. 5 covers cash markets, futures markets, options markets, and contract types; Ch. 21 discusses choosing between futures and stock markets.

title: Technical Analysis
author: Charles D. Kirkpatrick II, Julie R. Dahlquist
notes: Present through sentiment and behavioral-finance framing: Ch. 7 covers human bias, crowd behavior, contrary opinion, and sentiment indicators; Ch. 15 links behavioral finance to pattern recognition.

title: Margin of Safety
author: Seth A. Klarman
notes: Central concept. Chapter 6 is explicitly titled “Value Investing: The Importance of a Margin of Safety,” and the book frames value investing around buying below underlying value to protect against valuation error, bad luck, and uncertainty.

title: Margin of Safety
author: Seth A. Klarman
notes: Centrally taught through Chapter 8, “The Art of Business Valuation,” covering present-value analysis, private-market value, liquidation value, and conservative appraisal of underlying business value.

title: Margin of Safety
author: Seth A. Klarman
notes: Chapter 5/7 frame investing around risk aversion, loss avoidance, and requiring expected return to more than compensate for risk; the book explicitly says alternatives with risk are only superior if return fully compensates for that risk.

title: Margin of Safety
author: Seth A. Klarman
notes: The book repeatedly emphasizes disciplined value-investing process: know why an investment is undervalued, sell when the reason no longer applies, search for catalysts, and follow a repeatable research/evaluation process.

title: Margin of Safety
author: Seth A. Klarman
notes: Chapter 6 teaches the patience and discipline required to wait for bargains, stand apart from the crowd, and avoid speculation; this is presented as a core difficulty of value investing.

title: Margin of Safety
author: Seth A. Klarman
notes: Chapter 13 is identified as covering portfolio management, and the book explicitly advises investors to diversify holdings and hedge when financially attractive.

title: Margin of Safety
author: Seth A. Klarman
notes: Present but mainly as a tool inside valuation and distressed-security analysis: balance sheets, liabilities, seniority, cash-flow distortions, off-balance-sheet assets/liabilities, and accounting manipulation are discussed.

title: Margin of Safety
author: Seth A. Klarman
notes: The book discusses private-market-value multiples, takeover multiples, price-to-earnings, price-to-book, and related valuation yardsticks, but usually as inputs to conservative valuation rather than as a standalone framework.

title: Margin of Safety
author: Seth A. Klarman
notes: ubstantial secondary coverage through junk bonds, financially distressed companies, bankruptcy, debt-service requirements, creditor priority, and reorganization analysis. Stronger as distressed-debt investing than as broad macro/credit-cycle education.

title: Margin of Safety
author: Seth A. Klarman
notes: Chapter 13 discusses trading and selling decisions, liquidity, market depth, and why stop-loss orders can be flawed for value investors, but execution mechanics are not the book’s central teaching.

title: Security Analysis
author: Benjamin Graham, David Le Fevre Dodd
notes: Central coverage. Part V is entirely “Analysis of the Income Account,” covering income account analysis, extraordinary losses, misleading accounting artifices, depreciation, amortization, reserves, earnings records, capitalization structure, and sources of income. Part VI is “Balance-Sheet Analysis,” covering book value, current-asset value, liquidating value, and asset-value implications. Ch. XXXI–XLV.

title: Security Analysis
author: Benjamin Graham, David Le Fevre Dodd
notes: Central concept. Ch. I is explicitly “The Scope and Limitations of Security Analysis: The Concept of Intrinsic Value,” and Part VII later focuses on “Discrepancies Between Price and Value.” Ch. I and Ch. L–LI.

title: Security Analysis
author: Benjamin Graham, David Le Fevre Dodd
notes: Direct chapter-level coverage. Ch. XXXIX is “Price-Earnings Ratio for Common Stocks,” Ch. XLI covers low-priced common stocks and sources of income, and Ch. XLIX is “Comparative Analysis of Companies in the Same Field.”

title: Security Analysis
author: Benjamin Graham, David Le Fevre Dodd
notes: Central coverage through the analysis of earning power, income quality, past earnings records, rejected earnings records, depreciation/amortization charges, reserves, and capitalization structure. Ch. XXXI–XLI

title: Security Analysis
author: Benjamin Graham, David Le Fevre Dodd
notes: The book systematically covers bonds, preferred stocks, income bonds, guaranteed securities, convertible issues, senior securities with warrants, participating issues, common stocks, stock dividends, and stock-option warrants. Ch. V; Parts II–IV and VII.

title: Security Analysis
author: Benjamin Graham, David Le Fevre Dodd
notes: Strong central coverage of fixed-value investments, bond standards, railroad/public utility bonds, senior securities, guaranteed securities, protective covenants, and creditor remedies. This is mainly security-level credit/debt analysis rather than macro crisis theory. Part II and Part III.

title: Security Analysis
author: Benjamin Graham, David Le Fevre Dodd
notes: Central Graham-Dodd safety principle. The index explicitly lists “Margin of safety” across multiple sections, and the book repeatedly frames investment selection around safety of principal, adequate coverage, conservative valuation, and protection against adverse outcomes. Ch. VI–XI, Ch. XXVII, and later notes.

title: Security Analysis
author: Benjamin Graham, David Le Fevre Dodd
notes: Present through the distinction between investment and speculation, safety versus return, bond safety standards, and whether prospective profit compensates for risk. Important, but not formalized as a modern expectancy framework. Ch. IV, Ch. VI–XI, Introduction.

title: Security Analysis
author: Benjamin Graham, David Le Fevre Dodd
notes: Present through qualitative factors, management, sources of income, company comparison, and corporate structure analysis, but the book does not centrally teach modern “moat” or competitive-advantage analysis. Ch. II, Ch. XLI, Ch. XLVII–XLIX.

title: Security Analysis
author: Benjamin Graham, David Le Fevre Dodd
notes: Discusses investors, speculators, bondholders, stockholders, investment banking houses, management, and the public, especially in relation to 1927–1933 market behavior and financing standards. Secondary to valuation/security analysis. Introduction, Ch. IV, Ch. XLIV, Ch. XLVII.

title: Security Analysis
author: Benjamin Graham, David Le Fevre Dodd
notes: The book studies discrepancies between price and value and contrasts market analysis with security analysis, but it does not centrally teach modern market efficiency theory. Ch. L–LII.

title: Security Analysis
author: Benjamin Graham, David Le Fevre Dodd
notes: Present mainly through supervision of holdings, diversification-like safety logic, senior security safety, and avoiding overexposure to weak issues. It is not a modern portfolio-risk framework. Ch. XXI, Ch. XXVI, Ch. XLIV.

title: Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits
author: Philip A. Fisher
notes: Central concept. Ch. 3 “What to Buy: The Fifteen Points to Look for in a Common Stock” and Part Two “Conservative Investors Sleep Well” teach management quality, sales organization, research ability, production skill, cost control, competitive position, and business characteristics. The appendix also lists “Key Factors in Evaluating Promising Firms,” including functional factors, people factors, and business characteristics.

title: Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits
author: Philip A. Fisher
notes: Central coverage. Ch. 3 evaluates long-term sales growth, profit margins, research productivity, sales effectiveness, production efficiency, cost controls, and financial skill. Part Two expands this through product development, marketing, research, and profit-margin durability.

title: Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits
author: Philip A. Fisher
notes: The book teaches a repeatable investment process: use “scuttlebutt,” apply the fifteen points, decide when to buy/sell, avoid common investor mistakes, and build an investment philosophy from experience. Key references: Ch. 2 “What ‘Scuttlebutt’ Can Do,” Ch. 3, Ch. 8–10, and Part Three “Developing an Investment Philosophy.”

title: Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits
author: Philip A. Fisher
notes: Central to Fisher’s growth-stock framework. Ch. 1 contrasts short-term bargains with long-term growth fortunes; Ch. 4 applies stock selection to investor needs; Ch. 6 “When to Sell and When Not To” emphasizes holding superior companies for long periods rather than selling because of short-term valuation discomfort.

title: Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits
author: Philip A. Fisher
notes: Chapter-level coverage through Ch. 6 “When to Sell and When Not To,” Ch. 8 “Five Don’ts for Investors,” Ch. 9 “Five More Don’ts for Investors,” and Part Three sections on contrary thinking, patience, avoiding the crowd, and learning from mistakes.

title: Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits
author: Philip A. Fisher
notes: Fisher discusses price-earnings ratios, high-P/E growth stocks, and when a high multiple may be justified by superior business characteristics. However, he does not teach a full multiples-based valuation framework; valuation is secondary to business quality and growth durability. References: Part Two, especially “The Fourth Dimension,” and Part Three case discussions.

title: Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits
author: Philip A. Fisher
notes: Present through discussion of buying companies whose future value is underestimated and avoiding overpayment, but the book does not teach formal intrinsic valuation models. Fisher’s approach is qualitative appraisal of long-term business value rather than explicit DCF-style valuation.

title: Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits
author: Philip A. Fisher
notes: Present but secondary. The book references balance sheets, earnings statements, profit margins, depreciation, research spending, and financial skill, but Fisher explicitly downplays purely accounting-statistical analysis compared with scuttlebutt and business-quality investigation. References: Ch. 4, Ch. 10, and Part Two “Financial Skill.”

title: Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits
author: Philip A. Fisher
notes: Fisher frames the ideal investment as “greatest total profit for the least risk” and repeatedly compares growth-stock upside with business-quality risk. However, the book does not teach a formal expectancy/risk-reward model. References: Ch. 4 and Part Two.

title: Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits
author: Philip A. Fisher
notes: Covered mainly through Fisher’s warning against over-diversification and his discussion of adequate minimum diversification. It is important but not a broad portfolio-construction treatment. Reference: Ch. 8 “Five Don’ts for Investors.”

title: Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits
author: Philip A. Fisher
notes: Present in Part Three through the section “The Fallacy of the Efficient Market” and the idea that major price moves happen when the financial community changes its appraisal of a company. Secondary because the book is not mainly a market-efficiency textbook.

title: Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits
author: Philip A. Fisher
notes: Likely covered in “When to Buy” and Part Three through discussions of market downturns, business-cycle forecasting, bear markets, and buying during pessimism, but Fisher mostly critiques macro timing rather than teaching cycle analysis directly. Needs human verification before strong tagging.

title: The Essays of Warren Buffett
author: Warren Buffett
notes: Central coverage in Part V, “Accounting and Taxation,” especially “Look-Through Earnings,” “Economic Goodwill Versus Accounting Goodwill,” “Owner Earnings and the Cash Flow Fallacy,” and “Segment Data and Consolidation.” The book explicitly frames financial statements as tools for judging value, obligations, and management performance.

title: The Essays of Warren Buffett
author: Warren Buffett
notes: Central coverage in Part V.E, “Intrinsic Value, Book Value, and Market Price.” Buffett defines intrinsic value as discounted cash that can be taken out of a business over its remaining life, while stressing estimation uncertainty.

title: The Essays of Warren Buffett
author: Warren Buffett
notes: Central to the book’s investment philosophy: Berkshire is described as concentrating capital in businesses with outstanding economic characteristics and first-rate managers; Part II.D–F develops the idea through value investing, intelligent investing, and business selection.

title: The Essays of Warren Buffett
author: Warren Buffett
notes: Core Graham-Dodd/Buffett principle in Part II, especially “Mr. Market” and “‘Value’ Investing: A Redundancy.” The book explains buying only when price is materially below value.

title: The Essays of Warren Buffett
author: Warren Buffett
notes: Central coverage in Part II.C, “Debunking Standard Dogma,” and the Mr. Market discussion. The book directly critiques efficient-market assumptions, beta, volatility-as-risk, and price-value equivalence.

title: The Essays of Warren Buffett
author: Warren Buffett
notes: Central in Part II.C, “Debunking Standard Dogma.” The book teaches that true risk is permanent loss or business impairment, not beta/price volatility, and evaluates return relative to business quality, debt, taxes, and inflation.

title: The Essays of Warren Buffett
author: Warren Buffett
notes: Secondary but meaningful. Part III.C, “Dividend Policy,” and Part V.C–D discuss retained earnings, incremental returns on capital, owner earnings, economic goodwill, and whether growth actually creates value.

title: The Essays of Warren Buffett
author: Warren Buffett
notes: Present but not the main teaching target. The book contrasts long-term index investing for many people with focused, business-like active investing within one’s competence.

title: The Essays of Warren Buffett
author: Warren Buffett
notes: Secondary coverage through specific sections on common stock, junk bonds, zero-coupon bonds, preferred stock, and arbitrage. The book teaches these mainly through Buffett’s investment examples, not as a full market-foundations survey.

title: The Essays of Warren Buffett
author: Warren Buffett
notes: Secondary coverage in “Junk Bonds,” “Zero-Coupon Bonds,” and “Leveraged Buyouts.” The book critiques excessive debt, weak credits, and structures that hide future cash obligations.

title: The Essays of Warren Buffett
author: Warren Buffett
notes: Present through the long-term owner mindset in Part III, “Common Stock,” especially the idea of being willing to own a business even if the exchange were closed. This is more time-horizon focused than full goal-based planning

title: One Up On Wall Street
author: Peter Lynch
notes: Central thesis: individual investors can exploit advantages Wall Street often misses; covered in “The Advantages of Dumb Money,” Ch. 2 “The Wall Street Oxymorons,” and discussion of ignoring hot tips/brokerage recommendations.

title: One Up On Wall Street
author: Peter Lynch
notes: Core stock-selection lens: Ch. 8 “The Perfect Stock,” Ch. 9 “Stocks I’d Avoid,” and Ch. 15 “The Final Checklist” emphasize simple businesses, niches, low/no debt, buybacks, insider ownership, and avoiding poor-quality/trendy companies.

title: One Up On Wall Street
author: Peter Lynch
notes: Ch. 7 “I’ve Got It, I’ve Got It—What Is It?” and Ch. 10 “Earnings, Earnings, Earnings” teach classifying companies by growth profile and tying stock performance to sales/profit/earnings growth.

title: One Up On Wall Street
author: Peter Lynch
notes: Ch. 13 “Some Famous Numbers” teaches P/E, growth-rate comparison, dividend-adjusted P/E logic, cash-adjusted price, and judging whether a stock is overpriced or cheap relative to earnings/growth.

title: One Up On Wall Street
author: Peter Lynch
notes: Ch. 12 “Getting the Facts” and Ch. 13 teach reading annual reports, balance sheets, cash, securities, long-term debt, debt reduction, net cash, shares outstanding, and debt-to-equity.

title: One Up On Wall Street
author: Peter Lynch
notes: Ch. 11 “The Two-Minute Drill,” Ch. 14 “Rechecking the Story,” and Ch. 15 “The Final Checklist” teach building a clear investment thesis, monitoring whether the story remains true, and doing regular research before acting.

title: One Up On Wall Street
author: Peter Lynch
notes: Part III “The Long-Term View” and Ch. 16 “Designing a Portfolio” stress realistic long-term expectations, staying with a strategy through good and bad years, and judging performance over years rather than short-term price movement.

title: One Up On Wall Street
author: Peter Lynch
notes: Present in Ch. 16 through realistic return expectations, comparing individual stock-picking against index returns, and warning against taking unnecessary risks for unrealistic payoffs; useful but not as deeply formal as a portfolio theory text.

title: One Up On Wall Street
author: Peter Lynch
notes: Covered through “Passing the Mirror Test,” Ch. 18 “The Twelve Silliest (and Most Dangerous) Things People Say About Stock Prices,” and warnings against panic-selling after declines; important but secondary to the stock-picking framework.
